statement: A bag holds 6 red, 8 blue and 10 yellow balls. Without looking, Sam takes balls out one at a time. How many balls must he take to be certain of having at least two balls of each colour?

choices.misconception: I took two of each colour, as if Sam could choose which balls come out.
I allowed for all the yellow and blue balls coming out first and then made sure of only one red ball, but two are needed.
I let all the yellow balls come out first and then took two of each other colour, but all the blue balls could come out too.
I let all the yellow and blue balls come out first and forgot that he still needs two red ones.

hints: Imagine the unluckiest possible order of draws.
Worst-case counting: the colour that arrives last should be the one with the fewest balls. Count how many balls could come out before Sam has two of that colour.
All 10 yellow and all 8 blue balls could come out before any red ball.

solutions.reliable: In the worst case all 10 yellow and all 8 blue balls come out first, and Sam still has no red ball. He then needs 2 red balls, so $10 + 8 + 2 = 20$. With 19 balls, the bad case of 10 yellow, 8 blue and 1 red is possible, so 19 is not enough. With 20 balls, at most 18 are yellow or blue, so at least 2 are red; at most 16 are red or yellow, so at least 4 are blue; and at most 14 are red or blue, so at least 6 are yellow. The transferable idea: in a worst-case question, build the unluckiest sequence, then show that one more draw always breaks it.

whyOnTest: Certainty questions need the unluckiest case, and the trap is forgetting that two whole colours can be used up first.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
